speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the history. To better understand your post-tympanoplasty pain, can you describe the nature of the shooting pain and how it relates to the weight or pressure of earrings?

speaker: Patient
text: 25-year-old female. The patient has a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome, depression, and chronic bilateral ear infections. She underwent right ear tympanoplasty 12 weeks ago. Although audiology report from one week ago showed improved hearing by 20 decibels, she reports occasional shooting pain when eating and discomfort when wearing earrings. She describes her job as stressful and mentions poor sleep quality.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details; the shooting pain upon eating could suggest referred otalgia from a sensitive Eustachian tube or TMJ issue, but the discomfort with earrings warrants checking for graft displacement or granulation tissue. Did you notice any drainage, fever, or a change in hearing since your last audiology appointment? REQUEST TEST: Otoscopic examination and tympanometry.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Otoscopic examination reveals a patent right tympanic membrane with no evidence of active drainage or graft displacement. Tympanometry shows Type B flat trace in the right ear with normal acoustic reflexes, indicating stable middle ear pressure post-tympanoplasty. No fever or acute inflammatory signs observed.

speaker: Doctor
text: The otoscopic findings are reassuring regarding the graft, but the Type B tympanometry suggests middle ear effusion or fixation. Given your history of chronic ear infections and the "shooting" pain triggered by eating, is the pain also localized to your jaw joint or does it radiate specifically to the ear canal? REQUEST TEST: MRI Temporal Bone with contrast. REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Temporal_Bone

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI Temporal Bone with contrast shows no evidence of cholesteatoma, ossicular erosion, or graft displacement. Post-tympanoplasty middle ear space appears clear of fluid collections. The internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle are unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Since the MRI rules out structural complications like cholesteatoma or graft issues, and your Type B tympanometry suggests fluid fixation, could you clarify if the shooting pain feels like it originates from your teeth or gums when you eat, rather than just the ear? Additionally, have you noticed any clicking, popping, or tenderness in your jaw joint (TMJ) when you open your mouth wide?

REQUEST TEST: Dental X-Ray and Clinical TMJ Exam.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dental X-Ray reveals even and symmetric molar teeth bilaterally with no evidence of cavities, periapical pathology, or referred odontogenic pain. Clinical TMJ Exam shows no jaw clicking upon movement and no tenderness with palpation of the mandibular area.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the normal dental and TMJ exams, along with the Type B tympanometry and post-tympanoplasty history, could you describe the exact location of the pain on the ear exam and whether you have any numbness or tingling in the V3 distribution of your face? REQUEST TEST: Auriculotemporal Nerve Block and Facial Sensory Mapping.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Auriculotemporal Nerve Block provides temporary relief of the shooting pain associated with eating, confirming the pain pathway involves the auriculotemporal nerve. Facial sensory mapping reveals decreased light touch sensation in the right V3 (mandibular) distribution, specifically in the preauricular and tragus regions, consistent with post-surgical neural irritation or neuropathic otalgia.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Post-surgical auriculotemporal neuralgia (neuropathic otalgia) secondary to tympanoplasty.

The temporary relief from the nerve block combined with the sensory deficits in the V3 distribution confirms irritation of the auriculotemporal nerve, likely due to surgical trauma or scar tissue formation. The Type B tympanometry suggests concurrent middle ear effusion, which may be contributing to the discomfort, but the primary driver of your "shooting" pain is neuropathic rather than structural infection or graft failure.
